verdict: Caution: lend selectively to Kishangarh processors with documented slurry disposal and clean consents; avoid disposal-led units until NGT/CPCB rules settle.
title: Kishangarh stone, granite & marble processing: a note to the credit manager
narrative:
## What the business physically is
**Kishangarh runs on slurry: about 1,200 processing units feed a dump taking 5,500-6,000 tonnes of marble waste a day [2].** A processor buys blocks, cuts and polishes them into slabs and tiles, and sells to builders, exporters and traders; cash comes in on slab sales, but the physical residue leaves daily and must be stored or reused. **Value sits in finished, tested slabs and in proven chain of custody, not in raw cutting capacity [2].** Cost is dominated by block purchase, power and polishing consumables; pricing power is thin for commodity slabs and better for premium, tested product. Working capital is inventory-heavy (block and slab stock) plus receivables from builders; capex is in gangsaws, polishing lines and now lined slurry storage. **So when a proposal lands, check the slurry disposal plan and Consent to Operate first; if disposal is undocumented, ask where the slurry physically goes and who owns that land.**

## What has changed now
**The National Green Tribunal case and CPCB draft guidelines (lined storage, GPS-tracked transport, utilisation plans in each Consent to Operate) put direct regulatory pressure on the sector [2].** The guidelines remain draft and no monetary penalty was imposed on KMA in the judgment located [2], so this is a compliance-cost event, not yet a shutdown event. **Local stress is real: Rajasthan GST collections are -4.7% Apr-to-date against India +6.1%, and state electricity demand +4.0% against India +9.5% [D].** India-wide stone output is +11.4% YoY and +10.2% Apr-to-date [D], so the national trade is growing while this state lags. **Sources say little specific about Kishangarh's own sales or margins; lean on first principles and peers here.**

## Where the growth is
**Peer results show volume recovery and price realisation doing the work: Midwest's 4QFY26 revenue was INR2.2b, down 6% YoY but up 68% QoQ on volume and price recovery, with blended granite ASP at INR60,792/cbm [4].** Its 1QFY27 revenue was INR1.9b, up 35% YoY [5]. **Pursue processors who can show tested product, documented reuse and chain of custody [2], and units near group-owned quarries, which cut raw-material risk [11].** Avoid disposal-led processors without documented reuse [2], and treat export-concentrated units carefully: one rated peer is constrained by high geographical concentration in Europe [9]. Aro's June 2026 quarter net sales fell 23.72% YoY to Rs 20.62 crore [6] — a reminder that even established processors swing hard.

## How to grow safely
**Structure against the slurry liability, not just the slab stock: take the Consent to Operate, the disposal contract and the reuse plan as conditions precedent.** Covenant on compliant storage and GPS-tracked transport once guidelines firm up [2]. **Take monthly stock and debtor statements, power bills and GST returns; ask for the slurry-lifting log every month.** Keep fund-based limits sized to the inventory cycle, and note that a rated peer used only about 56% of its sanctioned working-capital limits in Jan-Dec 2025 [8] — utilisation tells you whether the limit is right-sized. **Price for compliance capex: lined storage is coming, so size repayment to absorb it.**

## Early-warning signs
- **Slurry dump volumes or lifting logs stop matching production (monthly) -> ask for the disposal contract and hold fresh limits.**
- **GST turnover falls below the Rajasthan trend of -4.7% [D] (monthly) -> reprice or reduce limit.**
- **Power bills drop without a stated shutdown (monthly) -> check whether cutting lines have stopped.**
- **Receivables past 90 days rise or slab stock ages (monthly) -> shift to stock-and-receivable-backed limits.**
- **Any NGT or CPCB order naming the borrower's unit (event-based) -> freeze enhancement and review consent status [2].**
